# Zone

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

Which region of the plot should the values stay inside? `zone` shades a
rectangle. It is [`rule`](rule.qmd)'s sibling: a rule draws a line and a zone
shades a region, and both work the same way. A rule takes one *position* and
spans the axis it was not given. A zone takes a *pair* and spans the axis it was
given no pair for. Give it pairs on both axes and it is a rectangle you placed.

Spanning the axis you gave no pair for is what first sets this mark apart. No
other mark draws a rectangle that reaches the edge of the **panel**, the region
inside the axes where the data is drawn.

## A band across the panel {#a-band-across-the-panel}

Were sales inside the target each year? You could print the two target numbers
in the caption. A reader would then have to check one year at a time. A band
shaded behind the line shows every year together.
The `quarterly` table holds one sales figure for each year, and `target_band`
holds the two edges of a target band:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(quarterly)
peek(target_band)
```

Here are the sales with the target band behind them, 150 to 175, across every
year the table holds:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper, and
also a line and points."*

`bounds(lower, upper)` names the two columns holding the bottom and top. Nothing
names a left or a right, so the zone takes those from the panel and runs edge to
edge. The zone is written *before* the line so the data draws on top of it; a
highlight belongs behind what it highlights.

## A band up the panel {#a-band-up-the-panel}

Some highlights are periods of time rather than ranges of value. The years of a
recession are one such period, when the question is how sales changed during
them. Name the other pair, `start` and `end`, and the rectangle runs up the
panel instead of across it. This pair is written by name. In `start = start`,
the first `start` is the side, and the second is the column in `recessions`.
The names are needed because two unnamed columns bound `y`, as `lower` and
`upper` did. The `recessions` table holds the two slumps, each with a start
year and an end year:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(recessions)
```

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "indianred") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end, and
also a line and points."*

Two shaded periods, and only one `zone` in the sentence. One row is one
rectangle, so a two-row table draws two bands. The same property lets one
`rule` table draw [three thresholds](rule.qmd#a-line-at-a-threshold). Add a row
and a third band appears with no change to the sentence.

Look at where the red reaches: the top and bottom of the panel exactly. That is
the thing a `ribbon` cannot do. A ribbon is bounded by its data, so it stops at
whatever numbers you give it. Any number big enough to reach the top would
*widen the axis to include it*, so the highlight would change the plot it was
meant to mark.

A ribbon does not take the `start`/`end` pair either. In the sentence below,
the ribbon runs along `x`, the years. At each year it has a bottom and a top,
but it has no left or right side for `start` and `end` to set, so gog refuses
the sentence. Its table is one row, written inside the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(data.frame(year = 2008, sales = 100, start = 2007.5, end = 2009.5),
     name = "slump") +
  x(year) + y(sales) + ribbon * bounds(start = start, end = end)
```

The message suggests `zone`, the mark that shades a rectangle.

The pair is called `start`/`end` rather than `left`/`right` on purpose. Left and
right are facts about a screen. This grammar takes orientation from the
bindings, so the same words still apply when `x` is drawn as an angle, in
[polar](../polar.qmd) coordinates.

## Both pairs: a rectangle {#both-pairs-a-rectangle}

Sometimes the region to highlight is bounded on both axes: these five years,
this range of sales, and nothing outside either. That is a rectangle closed on
all four sides, rather than a band across the panel.
Name all four and neither axis comes from the panel:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(sales_box)
```

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(lower, upper, start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A rectangle over five years of sales")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a sales box zone from lower to upper
and from start to end, and also a line and points."*

So one atom covers the three shapes a highlight needs: a band across the panel,
a band up it, and a rectangle bounded on both axes. The pairs you name decide
which one you get, so there is no separate atom for each.

## Which axis the pair bounds: the funnel {#which-axis-the-pair-bounds-the-funnel}

A funnel counts how many people are left at each stage, from website visits
down to invoices sent. Its usual picture is centered blocks, one per stage, one
above the other, measured across the page rather than up it. Drawing it means
putting the measurement on `x`, and putting a category on `y` does that.

The first two arguments of `bounds()` bound the *measure* axis, the axis that
carries the measured numbers. In the sales plots they were the columns `lower`
and `upper`. Every plot to this point has measured along `y`, so every such band
has run across the panel. Now put a category on `y` instead. The measure moves
to `x`, and the first two arguments of `bounds()` bound it there.

The `sales_funnel` table holds the five stages and `n`, the number of people at
each stage, in thousands. A funnel's blocks are centered on zero, so `lo` holds
`-n/2` and `hi` holds `n/2`. gog does not compute these columns: for a funnel of
your own, compute them in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript before the plot. `mid`
is 0 in every row, the place where each count is written:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(sales_funnel)
```

```{r}
data(sales_funnel) + zone * bounds(lo, hi) + y(stage) + style(opacity = 1) +
  text + label(n) + x(mid) +
  x_label("") + y_label("Stage") + title("A funnel, and no funnel atom")
```

*"Given the sales funnel: zones from lo to hi, y is stage, and also text, x is
mid, label by n."*

That is a funnel chart. Read it from the top: 39 thousand people visited the
website, and 2 thousand were sent an invoice, about one in twenty. No atom in
the sentence is a funnel.

Each block is a `zone`, drawn from one row of the table. The numbers inside the
blocks are a second layer, drawn by `text`. The waterfall's table, later in this
chapter, also holds both ends of each block, computed before the plot.

A funnel is a bar chart whose blocks are centered on zero. A `bar` grows from a
baseline and refuses `bounds`, so the centered blocks are zones with both ends
named.

The plot works because the first two arguments of `bounds()` name the measure
axis, not the bottom and the top of a screen. gog never asks which way the
screen runs; it asks what each axis carries. Here `y` carries a category, so
`y` is divided into **slots**, one part of the axis for each category. The
measurement can only go on `x`.
This is the rule [`bar`](bar.qmd) already follows: one categorical position, one
measured position, and their types decide the orientation. It is why there is
nothing like ggplot2's `coord_flip()` to write.

## Coloring the zones {#coloring-the-zones}

The two recession bands in the sales plot are both the same red, which leaves
them unnamed. Color each by its name and the legend says which is which,
with no note on the plot.
Each row is its own rectangle, so `color` maps per row. `recessions` carries a
name for each slump:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) + color(slump) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end
colored by slump, and also a line and points."*

A zone's `color` also takes a continuous column, giving each value a color from
a ramp, while `bar`, `area` and `ribbon` take only categories in `color`. A bar,
an area and a ribbon already show a number by their length or by their edges. A
heatmap cell shows no number by its size or edges: its shade, read against the
legend, is the measurement. So a
heatmap cell is this mark rather than a new one. [Cells cut from the
data](#cells-cut-from-the-data-the-heatmap) draws that plot, after the sections
on rectangles you place yourself.

## Rectangles that *are* the data {#rectangles-that-are-the-data}

The funnel's blocks were the data, but every other zone so far has been a
highlight: a rectangle behind a line, saying where to look. Nothing requires it
to be behind anything. Give a zone a pair on the measure axis and a
categorical position. Each category's rectangle then runs from one number to
another, with no plot underneath. Two common finance charts are made of exactly
that.

### The waterfall {#the-waterfall}

A **waterfall** is a running total, broken into the steps that made it. Each
block starts at the total before it, so the length of a block is the change in
its step, not the total. A `bar` with the
[`cumulative` transform](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total) draws
each total from zero, so it cannot draw a block that starts at the total before
it.
Where each block starts and ends is arithmetic on the table, done before the
plot. The `cashflow` table holds one row per step of a cash statement: a `delta`
for the step, and a `total` column that is TRUE for the opening and the closing
balance.

The `cash_blocks` table is `cashflow` with five columns computed from it. `top`
is the running total of `delta`, where each block ends. `base` is the running
total before the step, where the block starts. The Opening and Closing rows
start at zero. `dir` names each step a gain, a loss or a total. `left` and `right` are the
sides of each block, which the paragraphs after the plot explain:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(cash_blocks, n = 6)
```

```{r}
data(cash_blocks) + zone * bounds(base, top, start = left, end = right) +
  x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(c("steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred")) +
  y_label("Cash (thousands)") + title("Where the money went")
```

*"Given the cash blocks: zones from base to top and from left to right, x is
step, color by dir, with opacity 1."*

The whole chart is five computed columns and one sentence. The blocks that
start at zero are not a special case. They are rows whose `base` is 0, a number
the table supplies like every other.

Two parts of that sentence need explaining, because both override one of this
mark's defaults on purpose.

`style(opacity = 1)` is there because a zone whose sides you named is drawn
translucent, at 20%. A rectangle someone chose is nearly always a highlight,
with something drawn over it. Here nothing is drawn over it: the rectangle *is*
the measurement. A cut zone (a [heatmap](#cells-cut-from-the-data-the-heatmap)
cell) is already opaque for the same reason, and this is how you say the named
one is data too.

The `left`/`right` pair makes the gap between the blocks. Without `start` and
`end`, a zone fills its slot whole, while a [bar](bar.qmd) takes four fifths of
it and leaves one fifth empty, which is what separates the categories. A zone's
width normally means something: it is the region the category owns. A waterfall
block's width means nothing, so it should leave a gap the way `bar` does, and
naming the sides is how to ask for one. Here is the same sentence without
`start = left` and `end = right`:

```{r}
data(cash_blocks) + zone * bounds(base, top) +
  x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(c("steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred")) +
  y_label("Cash (thousands)") + title("Without start and end, the blocks touch")
```

*"Given the cash blocks: zones from base to top, x is step, color by dir, with
opacity 1."*

Each block now fills its slot and touches the next one: Sales and Refunds share
a side, and the other blocks meet at their corners. The six steps read as one
connected shape.

The `left` and `right` columns work because a categorical axis puts its
categories at 0, 1, 2 and so on. Category *k* owns the slot from `k−½` to
`k+½`, and `left` and `right` are `k ± 0.35`, inside it.

### The candlestick {#the-candlestick}

A **candlestick** shows how a price moved in each trading session. Each session
has four numbers: the price at the start (`open`) and the end (`close`), and the
highest (`high`) and lowest (`low`) prices in between. gog needs no new channels
for them, because a rectangle's sides read the pair a [ribbon](ribbon.qmd) and
an [interval](interval.qmd) already read. Low to high is a whisker, and open to
close is a rectangle, so the chart is two layers over one table.

The `candles` table is the `sessions` table with five columns computed from it.
`body_lo` and `body_hi` are the lower and the higher of `open` and `close`: the
bottom and the top of the **body**, the rectangle from open to close. `dir` is up
when the price closed at or above where it opened, and down otherwise. `left`
and `right` are `k ± 0.3`, computed as in the waterfall, so a body is 0.6 wide
where a waterfall block is 0.7:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(candles)
```

```{r}
data(candles) + x(session) +
  interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +
  zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) +
    color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(c("seagreen", "indianred")) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions")
```

*"Given the candles: x is session, intervals from low to high colored by dir,
and also zones from body lo to body hi and from left to right colored by dir."*

Read one session to see the two layers. Session 09 opened at 107.00 and closed
at 109.35, so its body is green and runs from 107.00 up to 109.35. Its whisker
runs from the session's low, 106.68, to its high, 109.62. Session 12 closed
below where it opened, so its body is red.

`color(dir)` is written twice, once after each mark. A channel such as `color`,
written after a mark, belongs to that mark alone
([scope](../encoding-scope.qmd)), so the first colors the whiskers and the
second the bodies. Both uses of the column share *one* legend, because it is
one column. Here is the chart with `color(dir)` after the zone only, beside the
chart above:

```{r}
(data(candles) + x(session) +
   interval * bounds(low, high) +
   zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) +
     color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
   palette(c("seagreen", "indianred")) +
   y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after the zone only")) |
  (data(candles) + x(session) +
     interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +
     zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) +
       color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
     palette(c("seagreen", "indianred")) +
     y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after each mark"))
```

*"Given the candles: x is session, intervals from low to high, and also zones
from body lo to body hi and from left to right colored by dir, beside the same
with the intervals colored by dir too."*

On the left, no `color` follows the interval, so every whisker is dark gray,
while the bodies are green and red. On the right, each whisker takes
its session's color, as session 12's red whisker shows.

There is no `candlestick` atom. The chart is made of atoms that already exist:
two marks, the `bounds` transform, the channels `x` and `color`, and the
settings `style` and `palette`.
[Chart names](../chart-names.qmd) lists it beside the pie and the rose, which
are also sentences rather than words.

## Cells cut from the data: the heatmap {#cells-cut-from-the-data-the-heatmap}

So far every zone has been a rectangle you *chose*, its sides named by columns
you already had. There is a second way to get sides, and it needs no new mark:
let `bin` cut them.

The `gm_all` table holds every Gapminder year: 142 countries, each measured in
12 years, so 1704 rows. Each row is one country in one year, a **country-year**.
Drawn as points, the crowded middle becomes one dark mass, because a thousand
dots in one place look exactly like two hundred. Cut the plane into cells and
count the rows in each instead. Here are the points beside the cells:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

```{r}
(data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("1704 country-years as points")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("The same rows, counted in cells"))
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life,
beside zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life."*

On the left, the upper part of the cloud, from about $3,000 to $30,000 and 65 to
80 years, is one solid patch of blue. On the right, the same patch is cut into
cells, and the darkest one, from about $6,800 to $8,700 and 70 to 73 years,
holds 40 country-years.

`bin` is not the zone's own transform. What the mark changes is how many axes
the cut runs along:

| Mark derived by `bin` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `bar * bin` | one axis cut, drawn as the bars of a histogram |
| `zone * bin` | two axes cut, drawn as the cells above |
| `surface * bin` | the same two axes, with the count raised into the cube |

Read the dark cells that rise from lower left to upper right: wealth and life
expectancy rise together. The darkest cell says how many country-years are at
that combination, which overlapping dots cannot show.

The same cells can show their counts as heights instead. Change the mark to
`bar` and add `space()`, and each cell becomes a separate bar rising in the
cube; the `surface * bin` row of the table joins the heights into one sheet
instead. [The 3-D histogram](../space.qmd#the-3-d-histogram) draws the heatmap
and the bars one after the other and compares what each one shows.

Three things in the heatmap's sentence need explaining: `bin` cut both axes,
the count became the color, and you can write that `color()` yourself.

`bin` cut both axes, and nothing asked it to. It is the same transform that
makes a histogram, and how many axes it cuts is taken from the mark rather than
requested. A `bar` leaves one axis free to measure a height along, so `bar *
bin` cuts the other one. A zone's cell needs an extent on *both* axes before it
can be a rectangle at all, so `zone * bin` cuts every axis that has a width to
cut, which here is both of them. One transform, one
word, readings decided by what the mark needs. There is no separate two-axis
bin, like ggplot2's `geom_bin_2d()`. Note the
words *has a width to cut*: [the mixed mesh](#one-of-each-the-mixed-mesh) is
where they matter, because a categorical axis is already cut, and `bin`
does not cut it.

The count became the color, although no `color()` was written. Both positions
were taken, so the measurement went to the one channel left that can carry a
number, and the legend is titled Count. This is what `bar * bin` already does
for the y axis: a transform that writes a column also says where it goes.

The column it writes is called `count`, and you may name it out loud. That is
not a different plot. It is the same sentence with nothing left implied:

```{r}
#| echo: false
run_spellings(
  r = r"---(short <- data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life)
long  <- data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
           color(count)

drawn <- function(plot) sub(' aria-label="[^"]*"', "", render_svg(plot))
identical(drawn(short), drawn(long)))---",
  python = r"---(import re

short = data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life)
long = (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
          color(col.count))

def drawn(plot):
    return re.sub(r' aria-label="[^"]*"', "", render_svg(plot), count=1)

print(drawn(short) == drawn(long)))---",
  julia = r"---(short = data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life)
long  = data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
          color(:count)

drawn(plot) = replace(render_svg(plot), r" aria-label=\"[^\"]*\"" => ""; count = 1)
println(drawn(short) == drawn(long)))---",
  js = r"---(const short = plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life));
const long = plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.count));

const drawn = (p) => render_svg(p).replace(/ aria-label="[^"]*"/, "");
console.log(drawn(short) === drawn(long));)---",
  tables = "gm_all"
)
```

`render_svg()` returns the picture as text. That text also holds a short
description of the plot for screen readers, written from the sentence. The long
form's description ends with "color by count", and the short form's does not.
The `drawn` function removes that description, and the rest of the two texts is
the same, so the two pictures are the same.

Naming `count` has one use: *a binding is where a scale goes*, and the short form
has nowhere to put one. Counts are strongly skewed here: the fullest cell holds
forty country-years while half of the cells hold four or fewer. On a linear ramp
nearly every cell is the same pale blue. Name the channel and you can say `scale =
"log"` on it, the same way you already did on `x`:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log
scale, y is life, color by count on a log scale."*

Now the cells with few rows get distinct shades, and the dark diagonal shows a
gradient rather than one flat patch of color. The legend's middle label is
6.32, not 20.5: on a log ramp the middle color stands for the geometric mean of
the two ends.

The empty gaps are cells where no country-year fell. They are left as panel,
not painted the pale end of the ramp, because that end stands for a count of
one. The uneven edge you get instead *is* the region the data actually covers,
which is information rather than a gap the renderer failed to fill.

`bin(24)` sets the **mesh**, the grid of cells the cut makes, exactly as it does
on a histogram, and one number cuts both axes into that many bins. A coarser
mesh shows less detail, and the plot looks less precise too:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 8, x is gdp on a log
scale, y is life."*

Notice that the log scale still applies. The cells are cut in log space, so
they are even on the page rather than even in dollars. That is what you want
when the variable ranges from a few hundred dollars to a hundred thousand.

These cells are also drawn solid rather than translucent, for the reason the
waterfall gave: here the zone *is* the data, with nothing behind it to show
through.

## Hexagons: the other mesh {#hexagons-the-other-mesh}

Does the grid pattern in a heatmap come from the data or from the mesh?
The cells above are rectangles, the default `tiling = "rect"`, and that is a
choice rather than a fact about binning. Say `tiling = "hex"` and the plane is
cut a different way. The two plots below differ only in `tiling`:

```{r}
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   palette("viridis") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("tiling = \"rect\", the default")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
     y(life) + palette("viridis") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("tiling = \"hex\""))
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is gdp on a log
scale, y is life, with the viridis palette, beside zones derived by bin into 20
on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette."*

Both plots also change two things from the first heatmap. `bin(20)` cuts a
little coarser than its `bin(24)`, and `palette("viridis")` replaces the
default ramp of blues. Viridis is the right choice for a count: it is built so
that equal steps in the number are equal steps in perceived brightness. On a plot whose entire message is *how many*, that is the difference
between reading the diagonal and guessing. The palette is a free choice on
either mesh, though, so do not read it as something hexagons require.

The hexagonal mesh is chosen for a reason, not for its looks: the rectangular
mesh has a defect. A rectangular grid lines up its cell centers in rows *and*
columns, and the eye is very good at seeing rows and columns: it reads that
alignment as if it were structure in the data. Wilkinson states it directly:
rectangular bins "lead the eye to align bin centers and to see regularity where
there is none" [@wilkinson2005]. That is why Carr and colleagues devised hexagon
binning in 1987 [@carr1987]. A hexagonal mesh staggers alternate rows, so there
is no aligned lattice left to mistake for a finding.

Look along the sparse edges of the two plots. The rectangular cells line up in
straight rows and columns, so the edge of the data is made of horizontal and
vertical pieces. The hexagons do not line up, so the edge has no long straight
pieces and follows the shape of the data more closely.

### Why the mesh belongs to `bin` {#why-the-mesh-belongs-to-bin}

In the rest of this book, a transform computes and the *mark* decides how the
result is drawn. `bar * bin`, `line * bin` and `step * bin` are one histogram
drawn three ways. So it would be reasonable to expect the hexagon to be a mark,
or a setting on one. It is neither, and the reason is in the numbers
themselves.

Those three marks all receive *the same* numbers. A hexagonal mesh staggers
alternate rows of cells, which changes *which cell each observation falls in*,
so the counts themselves differ. You cannot draw a hexagonal plot
from data binned into rectangles, whatever the mark does with it. The mesh is
decided before anything is drawn, so it belongs to the transform that does the
cutting.

That is also how Wilkinson organizes it. His `bin` is not one method but a
family of ways to partition a plane, with `rect` and `hex` among the members,
the two that gog's `tiling` takes.
The mesh both shapes the cells *and* tags each row with the cell it fell in. One
operation, both effects.

One consequence follows for the other marks: a tiling means nothing to a bin
that cuts one axis, because there the cells are intervals and an interval has no
shape. So gog refuses `bar * bin(tiling = "hex")`, and the message names
`zone` as the mark a tiling belongs to:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(life)
```

### Hexagons and the shape of the panel {#hexagons-and-the-shape-of-the-panel}

The hexagonal cells are not quite regular, meaning their six sides are not all
the same length. They are regular in the space the mesh is cut in, because that
cut gives both axes the same number of steps. The panel then stretches that
space by whatever its own proportions are, so on a wide panel the cells are
drawn slightly wide, and on a tall panel slightly tall. The pair above has tall
panels, and its hexagons are taller than they are wide.

R's `hexbin` package lets you set this stretch with its `shape` argument. A
panel kept at equal proportions removes it.
[`theme(ratio = 1)`](../style.qmd#theme-settings-that-belong-to-no-mark) asks
for that panel, and the hexagons are then regular:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") + theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Hexagonal cells on a square panel")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is
gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette, with ratio 1."*

The panel is now square, and each hexagon's six sides are the same length.

## Cells the data estimated: `zone * density` {#cells-the-data-estimated-zone-density}

Both meshes so far have counted the rows that fell in each cell. A count is
exact, but when the table is small, neighboring cells hold very different
counts. The `iris_flowers` table
holds 150 iris flowers, each with three measurements and its species.

`bin` counts the rows in each cell. There is a second thing worth measuring at
a cell, and it needs no new mark either: how dense the points are there. That
is `density`, the transform that gives a [line](line.qmd) its smooth curve. A
zone reads it across both axes, for the reason it reads `bin` across both. The
result is a **field**, a density estimated at every point of the plane. The zone
paints the field, and [`path`](path.qmd) traces the same field as contours.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

Here the 150 flowers are counted on the 24 × 24 mesh used above, beside the
density estimated from the same rows:

```{r}
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * bin(24) + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
   title("zone * bin(24): counted")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
     title("zone * density: estimated"))
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by bin into 24, x is sepal length, y is
petal length, beside zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal
length."*

Most of what the heatmap showed is true here too. The field was computed across
both axes without being asked, the measurement went to `color`, and
`color(density)` names it out loud and draws the identical plot. `zone * bin`
and `zone * density` are one plot measured two ways, counted and estimated.

One difference is easy to see. On the left, most of the cells are empty and
the fullest holds 6 flowers, so the two clusters break into scattered cells. On
the right, there are no empty cells, and each cluster is one smooth patch.
A count of zero says no row fell in that cell, so `bin` leaves it unpainted. An
estimate exists at every point of the plane, so the estimator returns a value
for every cell and the mesh is painted edge to edge. What it paints is a real
density rather than an arbitrary color value. The cell values times the cell
areas sum to one, the same property that makes the curve's `y` a density.

`palette()` chooses the ramp, exactly as it does for a binned heatmap, and the
argument for viridis on a count is the argument for it here:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density, viridis")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is
petal length, with the viridis palette."*

Look at the dark area away from the two clusters: it is even, and the cells meet
with no gaps. The SVG file tells the program that displays it to draw each
cell's edges sharp, on whole screen pixels, so no thin line of panel shows
between two cells.

One parameter a painted field takes is `adjust`. To estimate a density,
`density` places a small bell-shaped curve on each row and adds the curves up.
The width of each curve is the **bandwidth**, which gog computes from the data,
and `adjust` multiplies that width. It is a multiplier rather than a width in
either column's units, which is why it means the same thing on both axes:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(adjust = 1.6) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same flowers, smoothed more")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density adjusted by 1.6, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette."*

Compare it with the plot above. The two clusters are wider and blurrier, and
the space between them is no longer dark. The highest density in the legend
falls from 0.163 to 0.101, because each flower's curve is spread wider.

The second parameter is `places`: how many places along each axis the field is
computed at. The default is 64 on each axis. The places are the corners of the
cells, so 64 places make 63 × 63 cells. Fewer places draw larger cells and a
smaller file:

```{r}
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(places = 24) +
   x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
   title("density(places = 24)")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
     x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
     title("density, 64 places"))
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density at 24 places, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette, beside zones derived by
density, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette."*

The left heatmap has 23 × 23 cells, and its file is about 77 KB. The right one
has 63 × 63 cells and is about 545 KB. The file grows with the square of
`places`: about 2.2 MB at 128 places, and about 9 MB at 256, the most a field
takes. So raise `places` only when the cells are too coarse to read. [How many
places](../transforms.qmd#how-many-places-places) lists the default of every
reading of `density`.

The same field *traced* rather than painted is [`path * density`](path.qmd), the
contour. The difference between them is the one between `bar * bin` and `line *
bin`: the mark chooses the shape, and the transform stays the same.

## Bands the data cut: `zone * density(levels = )` {#bands-the-data-cut-zone-densitylevels}

A smooth ramp is hard to read a value from: two nearby cells differ by a shade
too small for the eye to see. Cut the field into a few steps and each band has a level a
reader can point to.
Ask for levels and the field stops being continuous. It is cut into that many
steps, and a zone fills between them:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density bands")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette."*

That is the **filled contour**, and `levels` is the same parameter `path` takes.
`levels` means one thing, cut the field into this many steps, and each mark then
draws that cut its own way: a path traces the boundaries, a zone fills between
them. So the two are not two features but one transform read by two marks, and
a band's edge falls exactly on the contour line:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal
length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette."*

That makes three readings of one transform: [`line * density`](line.qmd) is a
curve, `zone * density` a painted field, and `path * density` a contour.

The bands lie one inside another. A denser region usually lies *inside* a less
dense one, so gog paints the outermost band first and each inner band over it. A
band can also have a hole. When points lie around a circle, the density in the
middle is low, so each band has a hole there. gog cuts the hole out of the band,
and the middle stays unpainted.

## Cells the axes already made: the tile plot {#cells-the-axes-already-made-the-tile-plot}

So far the sides have been made in three ways: `bounds` named them, `bin` cut
them, and `density` estimated them. The funnel already used a fourth way without
naming it: a category's slot, which needs no columns for its sides.

The `six_weeks` table holds six weeks of daily orders, one row per day. Each day
has a week and a weekday, so the 42 counts already form a grid: weeks across,
weekdays down. The grid itself is the picture you want, and two categorical axes
already divide the panel into its cells.

A categorical axis is already divided. Six weeks on the x axis is six slots.
"Week 3" owns one of those slots, a place on the panel with a left edge and a
right edge, and the axis fixes both when it lays out the categories. So a
category bounds its own axis, and two categorical positions bound a zone
completely, with no transform in the sentence:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(six_weeks)
```

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + zone + x(week) + y(weekday) + color(orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: zones, x is week, y is weekday, color by orders."*

That is a **tile plot**, here in the form called a calendar heatmap, and the
whole of it is `zone + x + y + color`. What makes it worth drawing is that 42
daily counts carry two patterns at once, one by week and one by weekday. A list
of numbers shows neither, while a grid separates them by direction. Compare the
columns to see the weeks: week four is the palest, the lowest week. Compare the
rows to see the weekdays: the Thursday row is the darkest overall, and the
Friday row the palest. The extremes are the cells where the two patterns
agree: the darkest cell is Thursday of week six, and the palest are the Friday
and Saturday of week four.

The rule behind the tile plot is short: a category owns a slot, a number is a
point. A point has no width, so two continuous positions leave a zone with
nothing to bound it until a transform such as `bin` gives it sides. The tile
plot needed nothing new: no mark, no transform and no channel was added to the
kernel.

### `bin` cuts, `count` tallies {#bin-cuts-count-tallies}

The `six_weeks` table has one row per cell already. Often a table does not: you
hold the raw observations and want to know how many fell in each cell. The
`winds` table is one of these. Each row is one observation of the wind.
`direction` is where it blew from, one of eight compass points, and `bearing` is
the same direction in degrees. Each row also holds the wind's `speed` and the
`season`. The transform that tallies the rows in each cell is `count`, exactly
as it is for a bar chart:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(winds)
```

```{r}
data(winds) + zone * count + x(direction) + y(season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season")
```

*"Given the winds: zones derived by count, x is direction, y is season."*

That is the shape of a confusion matrix, the table that counts predicted classes
against actual ones. A confusion matrix is the same sentence with different
columns: `zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted)`.

Notice what was *not* needed there. `bin` cuts a continuous axis into cells
before anything can be counted in them; a categorical axis is already cut, so
there is nothing left to do but tally. `bar * bin` and `bar * count` follow
the same rule on one axis; here both axes follow it. So each refusal names the
other transform: give `zone * count` a continuous axis and it names `bin`, and
give `zone * bin` two categorical axes and it names `count`.

A tile plot has two categorical positions where a bar chart has one. That
second position changes only where the tally is written. A bar has a length to
put it on, so `bar * count` writes its tally to the y axis. A tile plot's two
positions are both taken by categories, so `zone * count` writes its tally to
`color`, and the legend is titled Count.

`proportion` is the same tally as a share of the whole, which is the plot to
draw when the absolute numbers are not what you want to read:

```{r}
data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(direction) + y(season) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares")
```

*"Given the winds: zones derived by proportion, x is direction, y is season."*

That share is of *every* row counted, not of a row or a column of the grid. A
confusion matrix divided by the total of each actual class needs a different
denominator. `proportion` always divides by the whole table, so compute each
class's shares in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript and draw them as a tile plot.

`proportion` reads a cut mesh the same way. Compose it with `bin` and the
heatmap's counts become shares of the whole, the [relative-frequency
histogram](../transforms.qmd#normalizing-something-other-than-a-tally) with a
second axis. The plot reads the `gm_all` table, shown in [Cells cut from the
data: the heatmap](#cells-cut-from-the-data-the-heatmap):

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 and proportion, x
is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette."*

`proportion` leaves the cells exactly where `bin` cut them, and the legend now
reads in shares. The legend's top value, 0.0264, is the share in the fullest
cell: 45 of the 1704 rows.

### `count` tallies rows, `mean` reduces a column {#count-tallies-rows-mean-reduces-a-column}

The wind table records more than which cell each observation fell in. Each row
also carries a `speed`, and the question "how fast, on average, in each cell?"
is not a tally at all; it is a summary of one column.

The first sentence to try is a plain tile plot, and it is refused. A `zone`
draws one opaque rectangle for each row, and here many rows share each cell.
Their rectangles would be drawn one on top of another, so each cell would show
only the color of its last row. gog counts the rows that would be hidden, and
names the summary to write instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)
```

`zone * mean` draws one rectangle for each cell, colored by the mean speed of its
rows:

```{r}
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed) +
  title("Mean wind speed, by direction and season")
```

*"Given the winds: zones derived by mean, x is direction, y is season, color by
speed."*

Compare that with `zone * count` in the section above. The sentence has the same
shape, with `mean` for `count` and one more binding. `count` was handed no
column, so it counts rows and labels the result `count`. `mean`
was handed one, and `color(speed)` says which column it reduced. All six
summaries read a mesh this way (`sum`, `mean`, `median`, `max`, `min` and
`quantile`), and each writes its answer back into the column it reduced.

[The heatmap](#cells-cut-from-the-data-the-heatmap) showed that the measurement
goes to `color` when both positions are taken. Color does a second job as well:
it is also the channel that names the column, because a summary writes its result back into the column it read. On an
ordinary two-axis bar chart, `bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)` names `life`
with `y` and puts the mean back on `y`;
the source and the destination are one binding. A zone measures by color, so
`color` is both the source and the destination.

The whole rule is short. A summary reduces the column on the channel that
carries the measurement: `y` on a bar, `color` on a zone. It groups by every
position that does not carry it. A bar measures with `y`, so it groups by `x`.
A zone measures with nothing positional, so it groups by both. In [the
cube](../space.qmd) a bar measures with `z`, so it also groups by both of the
other positions.

A summary composes with `proportion` too: each cell's summary becomes a share of
the total over all cells. The `titanic` table already holds counts: each row is a
group of people aboard, and `n` is the size of the group. So `sum` adds up the
people in each cell, and `proportion` turns each sum into a share of everyone
aboard. Counting rows would not answer the question here: `zone * proportion`
gives every cell 0.125, because each cell holds 4 of the table's 32 rows.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(titanic)
```

```{r}
data(titanic) + zone * sum * proportion + x(class) + y(survived) + color(n) +
  title("Everyone aboard, as shares: class by survival")
```

*"Given titanic: zones derived by sum and proportion, x is class, y is
survived, color by n."*

The legend is titled Proportion, because its numbers are now shares of everyone
aboard. `color(n)` still names the column that `sum` adds up. The darkest cell
holds the crew who did not survive: 0.306, about three in ten of everyone aboard.

Say `mean` with nothing for it to reduce and the engine asks for the column
rather than guessing, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

A summary also needs cells to summarize into. The six summaries measure without
cutting, so each axis must already be divided. [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows the refusal and the two ways to fix the
sentence.

### Cells cut, then summarized: the summary heatmap {#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap}

The last two sections let the axes supply the cells. This section and the next
put `bin` back in the sentence.
How does life expectancy depend on income and on time together? Both are
continuous, so neither axis is divided into cells yet. `bin` cuts them, and
`mean` measures inside each:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(15) * mean + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  color(life) + title("Mean life expectancy, by era and income")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 15 and mean, x is
year, y is gdp on a log scale, color by life."*

`bin(15)` cuts the plane into cells, `mean` reduces `life` inside each, and
`color` both names that column and carries the answer, exactly as it does on the
tile plot above. Read the panel from bottom left to top right and you can see
both patterns. Life expectancy rises with income up the panel, and rises
again with time across it. The three empty vertical strips are bins with no
year in them: the table measures every fifth year, and each of the fifteen bins
is less than four years wide.

`bin(15)` cuts the same cells with or without `mean`. What changes is the
color: with `mean`, it no longer shows how many rows fell in each cell. Without
`mean`, the same cells are counted:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(15) + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  title("The same cells, counted")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 15, x is year, y is
gdp on a log scale."*

Read it against the plot above: the count says how many observations fell in
each cell, and the mean says what those observations were like. The cells along
the top, the richest incomes before 1980, are the palest here: each holds one
country-year, and all five are Kuwait. In the mean plot the same cells look as
solid as any other, because a mean does not show how many rows it came from.

The same composition works when one axis is a category. Cut the income axis, and
leave the continents in their slots:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) * mean + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(continent) +
  color(life) + title("Mean life expectancy, by income band and continent")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is gdp
on a log scale, y is continent, color by life."*

One axis was cut and the other was already in slots, which is the mixed mesh
the next section states as a rule.

### One of each: the mixed mesh {#one-of-each-the-mixed-mesh}

How does the spread of life expectancy differ by continent? Five histograms
could answer it, in five panels the reader must compare one by one.
Read the tile plot's rule (a category owns a slot, a number is a point) one
axis at a time, and it already covers the case between the heatmap and the tile
plot: one axis continuous, one categorical. Nothing new has to be decided for it. `bin` cuts
the axis that has a width to cut, and not the one that is already cut, so the
result is a row of cells per category:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Life expectancy, a distribution per continent")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is life, y is
continent, with the viridis palette."*

That is a distribution shown as shade rather than as height, which is what makes
five of them fit in the space one histogram would take. Read a row and it is one
continent's histogram. Read the plot and you see the shape of each continent's
spread. Africa's mass is at the far left and Europe's at the far right. Asia spreads the
widest and Europe the narrowest of the four large rows, with Africa and the
Americas in between. Oceania has only two countries in this table, which is why
its row is the shortest.

Two things make it a mesh and not five plots side by side. Every row is cut on
*the same* edges: the bin edges are computed once from the whole `life` column,
never per category. So each column of cells covers the same range of life
expectancy for every continent, and the boundaries line up all the way down.
And an empty cell stays empty. Oceania's row starts at 69 years, its lowest
life expectancy, and the cells to its left are not painted the palest end of
the ramp. The uneven left edge shows where each continent's values begin.

Swap the axes and each distribution becomes a column instead of a row:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + y(life) + x(continent) + palette("viridis")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, y is life, x is
continent, with the viridis palette."*

Neither orientation needed anything new. Three cases, one rule read one axis at
a time:
`bin` cuts both axes in the heatmap and one in this plot, and the tile plot
needs no `bin` at all.

### One slot: a column highlight {#one-slot-a-column-highlight}

The wind blows most often from two of the eight directions, W and SW. A strip
plot draws each speed as a point above its direction. Shading those two
directions behind the points makes them easy to find.
Reading the tile plot's rule one axis at a time leaves one more case: a
category on one axis and nothing on the other. A zone bounded on *one*
categorical axis takes that slot and spans the panel on the other, which is
what this mark does whenever no column is written for an axis. One row is still one
rectangle, so the table you give it is the list of slots to shade. Here that
list is a table of two rows, one for each direction, written inside the
sentence:

```{r}
data(data.frame(direction = c("SW", "W")), name = "prevailing") + zone +
  x(direction) + style(color = "goldenrod") +
  data(winds) + point * jitter + x(direction) + y(speed) +
  y_label("Speed") + title("The two directions the wind actually comes from")
```

*"Given two rows with direction SW and W: zones, x is direction; then given the
winds: points derived by jitter, x is direction, y is speed."*

Nothing was built for that. It is the same sentence as the tile plot with one
axis left unsaid, which shows that a slot is a general way to get sides, not a
special case for one chart.

The two-row table does what [`rule`](rule.qmd)'s table does, and for the same
reason: a zone's position is a column, so one table shades as many slots as
it has rows. Give the zone the whole `winds` table instead, in a sentence with
no other layer, and it draws one rectangle per row: 264, one over another in
eight slots. That is what the rule says, and not the plot you wanted.

In the plot above, `winds` cannot replace the two-row table. A position is not
like `color`: written after one mark, it still reaches the other layers
([Encoding scope](../encoding-scope.qmd#the-rule)). `y(speed)` would reach the
zone, and a continuous `y` gives a zone no sides, so gog refuses the sentence.
The two-row table has no `speed` column, so the zone spans the panel from
bottom to top.

One difference is easy to see. The column highlight is translucent and the
calendar heatmap is not. A zone that spans the panel on one axis is a highlight,
and gog draws it at 20%. A zone whose cells come from the data on both axes is
the data itself, and gog draws it opaque. `style(opacity = )` overrides either.

## Sides the data drew: the choropleth {#sides-the-data-drew-the-choropleth}

In every section above except the filled contour, each rectangle takes its
sides from one row: a row of your table, or a row a transform made. `bounds`
names the sides, `bin` cuts them, `density` estimates them, and a category owns
a slot. There is a fifth way, where one shape takes its outline from many rows
of your own table.

A map with every country shaded is a plot most readers have seen, and a
country's shape is not a rectangle.
A boundary is a list of points around the edge of a region: a coastline, a
border, the outline of a sales territory. It is stored as one row per point, so
a single shape needs many rows, and the sentence needs a word for which
rows belong together. That word is `group`. The `world_borders` table holds one
row per point. Its `piece` column numbers a country's separate outlines, such
as its islands. The zone does not need it: gog ends each outline where it
returns to its first point, and `group(country)` fills all of a country's
outlines as one region
([Rings](../map.qmd#rings-and-the-country-inside-another-country)):

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(world_borders)
```

```{r}
data(world_borders) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) +
  color(continent) + map()
```

*"Given the world borders: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by country, color
by continent, in the map space."*

That is the **choropleth**. The mark is the same `zone`, and the kernel needs
no new atom. A zone is usually a rectangle, but its shape comes from whatever
gives its sides, and here a boundary gives them. A boundary gives a zone its
sides only in the [map](../map.qmd) space or on a globe, where the two positions
are longitude and latitude. On a plain panel, gog refuses `group` on a zone, and
the message suggests `map()` or `globe()`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(world_borders) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) +
  color(continent)
```

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a zone takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("zone")
```

A zone draws only with a transform marked ●, or with positions that give it its
sides. Two categorical positions give those sides, and so does one categorical
position with nothing on the other axis, so [the tile
plot](#cells-the-axes-already-made-the-tile-plot) and [the column
highlight](#one-slot-a-column-highlight) draw with no transform at all. So does
[the choropleth](#sides-the-data-drew-the-choropleth), whose sides are the
points of a boundary.

The plots below show every transform a zone takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change. Most of the transforms already have a section above, and the
paragraph before each figure links to it.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows in each cell, so on their
own they need a category on both positions. `bin` and `density` work on numbers. `bin` cuts
each continuous axis into cells and counts the rows in each. `density` needs two
numbers, and estimates how closely the rows lie in each cell. Both positions are
taken, so all four write their result to `color`. [`bin` cuts, `count`
tallies](#bin-cuts-count-tallies) shows the tally on its own. The top two plots
read the `winds` table, shown in that section, with `direction` on `x` and
`season` on `y`. The bottom two read the `iris_flowers` table, shown in [Cells
the data estimated](#cells-the-data-estimated-zone-density), with
`sepal_length` on `x` and `petal_length` on `y`:

```{r}
((data(winds) + zone * count + x(direction) + y(season) + title("zone * count")) |
  (data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(direction) + y(season) +
     title("zone * proportion"))) /
  ((data(iris_flowers) + zone * bin + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
      title("zone * bin")) |
     (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
        title("zone * density")))
```

*"Given the winds: zones derived by count, x is direction, y is season, beside
zones derived by proportion, x is direction, y is season; above zones from the
iris flowers, derived by bin, x is sepal length, y is petal length, beside zones
derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length."*

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows of each cell to one value. They
need a category on both positions, and `color()` naming the number to reduce,
because a zone shows its measurement in color. A number on a position needs
`bin` first, to cut it into cells, as in [the summary
heatmap](#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap). Five plots read the
wind `speed` in the `winds` table. They give the mean, the median, the largest
and the smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)` gives the speed that nine tenths of
each cell's observations fall below. The last plot reads the `titanic` table,
shown in [`count` tallies rows, `mean` reduces a
column](#count-tallies-rows-mean-reduces-a-column), with `class` on `x` and
`survived` on `y`. Its `sum` reads `n`, the number of people in each row,
because only an amount has a total that means something:

```{r}
(((data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season) +
     color(speed, limits = c(0, 28)) + title("zone * mean")) |
    (data(winds) + zone * median + x(direction) + y(season) +
       color(speed, limits = c(0, 28)) + title("zone * median"))) /
   ((data(winds) + zone * max + x(direction) + y(season) +
       color(speed, limits = c(0, 28)) + title("zone * max")) |
      (data(winds) + zone * min + x(direction) + y(season) +
         color(speed, limits = c(0, 28)) + title("zone * min"))) /
   ((data(winds) + zone * quantile(0.9) + x(direction) + y(season) +
       color(speed, limits = c(0, 28)) + title("zone * quantile(0.9)")) |
      (data(titanic) + zone * sum + x(class) + y(survived) + color(n) +
         title("zone * sum")))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given the winds: zones derived by mean, x is direction, y is season, color by
speed from 0 to 28, beside zones derived by median, x is direction, y is season,
color by speed from 0 to 28; above zones derived by max, x is direction, y is
season, color by speed from 0 to 28, beside zones derived by min, x is
direction, y is season, color by speed from 0 to 28; above zones derived by
quantile at 0.9, x is direction, y is season, color by speed from 0 to 28,
beside zones from titanic, derived by sum, x is class, y is survived, color by
n."*

Each plot in a figure builds its own color scale from its own values. The five
plots that read `speed` all write `limits = c(0, 28)`, so they share one range,
and a shade is the same speed in each of them. So when the `max` cells are
darker than the `min` cells, the speeds really differ.
[Scales](../scales.qmd#limits-stating-the-range-yourself) explains `limits`.

**Pairs.** `bounds` reads lows and highs that you computed yourself, as one
pair of columns or two. The pairs you name decide the shape. `lower` and
`upper` make a band across the panel, `start` and `end` make a band up the
panel, and all four make a rectangle bounded on both axes. [A band across the
panel](#a-band-across-the-panel), [A band up the panel](#a-band-up-the-panel)
and [Both pairs](#both-pairs-a-rectangle) draw each shape on its own. They also
show the `quarterly`, `target_band`, `recessions` and `sales_box` tables. Here
the three shapes are side by side, over the same sales:

```{r}
((data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
    data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) +
    data(quarterly) + line + title("zone * bounds: lower, upper")) |
   (data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
      data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
      data(quarterly) + line + title("zone * bounds: start, end")) |
   (data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
      data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(lower, upper, start = start, end = end) +
      data(quarterly) + line + title("zone * bounds: all four"))) +
  theme(height = 400)
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper, and
also a line, beside the same with recession zones from start to end instead,
beside the same with a sales box zone from lower to upper and from start to end
instead."*

**Layouts.** `partition`, `flow` and `cluster` read categorical columns and
arrange the whole picture at once. `partition` divides a whole among nested
categories. It needs one column for each level, from the top level down. A
number on a position sizes each part, here `x(amount)`; without one, each row
counts as one. `flow` stacks one slot for each category of each column it
names. The amount on `y`, here `y(n)`, sizes each slot; without it, each row
counts as one. These two compute each rectangle themselves, from the columns
named. `cluster` computes no rectangles: it reorders the slots of a tile plot,
so it needs the tile plot's two categories and its color. `over = nutrient` says that each food is compared by its amounts
of the five nutrients, so the foods on `x` are the slots that move. The
`spending` table is a household budget with one row for each leaf, meaning the
last level of a branch. The `nutrients` table holds five nutrients for each of
eight foods:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(spending)
peek(nutrients)
```

```{r}
(((data(spending) + zone * partition(group, item, detail) + x(amount) +
     color(group) + style(border_color = "white") + title("zone * partition")) |
    (data(titanic) + zone * flow(class, survived) + y(n) + title("zone * flow"))) /
   (data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over = nutrient) + x(food) + y(nutrient) +
      color(amount) + title("zone * cluster"))) +
  theme(height = 700)
```

*"Given the spending table: zones derived by partition through group, item and
detail, x is amount, color by group, beside zones from titanic, derived by flow
through class and survived, y is n; above zones from nutrients, derived by
cluster over nutrient, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount."*

The partition plot is the **icicle**: one row of rectangles for each level of
the budget. With `cross = TRUE`, `zone * partition` draws the
[mosaic](../transforms.qmd#the-mosaic) instead, where the second level divides
the height of each column of the first. The flow's zones are the slots that the
bands of a [flow diagram](../flow.qmd) leave and arrive at. The
[Cluster](../cluster.qmd) chapter draws the tree that decided the order of the
foods.

A zone refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. `smooth` and
`straight` fit a line, and `cumulative` adds a running total, which
[`line`](line.qmd), [`point`](point.qmd) and [`bar`](bar.qmd) draw. The other
pair transforms compute a low and a high from the rows, which
[`interval`](interval.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), [`line`](line.qmd) and
[`step`](step.qmd) draw. The collision
modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as [`bar`](bar.qmd),
[`point`](point.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd). `layout` places names as a network, which
[`edge`](edge.qmd), [`point`](point.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A highlight has to stay in the background, and a heatmap cell has to be solid.
gog gives each kind its own default, and a setting in `style()` overrides it for
the whole layer. Each mark takes its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a zone's settings,
with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("zone")
```

The table's five settings are what a filled shape with an outline takes: a
color, an opacity and a pattern for the fill, and a color and a width for the border. One of them
has a default that matters. `opacity` is 0.2 for a placed zone: one whose sides
you named with `bounds`, or one that spans the panel on an axis. It is 1 when
the data gives every side: cells `bin` cut, cells `density` estimated, the slots
two categories own, the regions a boundary gives, and the rectangles `partition`
and `flow` compute. A placed zone is a highlight. It stays pale so the gridlines, and any layer
written before it, show through. A zone of the second kind *is* the data, with
nothing behind it to reveal.

The next plot draws three bands behind the sales of the `quarterly` table, shown
in [A band across the panel](#a-band-across-the-panel). Each band reads a table
of one row, written inside the sentence, and adds one setting: a color, then an
opacity, then a hatch:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(data.frame(start = 2006, end = 2009), name = "early") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(data.frame(start = 2011, end = 2014), name = "middle") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "indianred", opacity = 0.55) +
  data(data.frame(start = 2017, end = 2020), name = "late") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "hatch", opacity = 0.7) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Color, then opacity, then a hatch")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales; then given one row with start 2006 and
end 2009: a zone from start to end, colored seagreen; then given one row with
start 2011 and end 2014: a zone from start to end, colored indianred, with
opacity 0.55; then given one row with start 2017 and end 2020: a zone from
start to end, colored steelblue, with pattern hatch and opacity 0.7; then given
quarterly again: a line and points."*

The default opacity keeps the first band pale with nothing set, so the line and
points stay the strongest marks on the page. Raise it when the zone is the
subject of the plot rather than its background, as the red band does here.

Use the hatch when a plot will be printed in gray, or when two overlapping zones
need more than color to separate them. Give it more opacity
than a flat fill needs, as the blue band does: a hatch is a set of lines with
gaps between them, so fading it to 0.2 leaves very little to see. A zone takes
the *fill* textures, not the stroke patterns. `style(pattern = "dashed")` on a
zone is refused, and the message lists the six fill textures instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(pattern = "dashed")
```

One setting you might expect is refused: `style(size = )`. A zone's bounds
already set how big it is, so there is no size left to set:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(size = 3)
```

A zone can be drawn with or without a **border**, and both are good choices. A
highlight behind a line reads better with no border. If you want its edges
drawn, two `rule`s do it better than a border: they can be dashed, and each is
at a real value on the axis. The target band comes from the `target_band` table,
shown in [A band across the panel](#a-band-across-the-panel). The rules read a
table of two rows, one for each edge, written inside the sentence:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(data.frame(sales = c(150, 175)), name = "edges") + rule +
    style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper; then
given two rows with sales 150 and 175: rules colored seagreen, with pattern
dashed; then given quarterly again: a line and points."*

The two marks read their positions differently, which is why the edges need a
table of their own. A zone is told which columns hold its sides, with
`bounds(lower, upper)`. A rule reads whichever of the plot's own position
columns its table carries, so the edges must be in a `sales` column. The rule
chapter draws the same two marks over a scatter of life expectancy, in
[Thickness as data](rule.qmd#thickness-as-data).

But the mark is not only a highlight. It draws the waterfall, the heatmap's
cells, [the icicle](../transforms.qmd#partition-a-whole-among-nested-parts) and
the [mosaic](../transforms.qmd#the-mosaic), and in every one of those the zone
*is* the data rather than a background behind it. There the composition above
cannot help. A rule spans the whole panel, or makes a short tick at its edge, so
it cannot outline one cell of a mosaic. So a zone takes `style(border_color = ,
border_size = )`, like `bar`, `box`, `point` and `surface`. The plot outlines the
two slumps of the `recessions` table, shown in
[A band up the panel](#a-band-up-the-panel):

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(border_color = "black") +
  data(quarterly) + line +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone with a border of its own")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end,
with border color black, and also a line."*

Both choices stay available, and which one is right depends on whether the zone
is the background or the subject. By default a zone has no border: with no
`border_color` and no `border_size`, it draws no outline.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

A `point` or a `line` draws from the plot's own `x` and `y`, so a bare `zone`
over the same table is the natural first attempt. Two continuous positions give
a rectangle no width and no height, so it is refused:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) + zone + line
```

A categorical column on one axis and a continuous one on the other do not make
a cell either. The category bounds its own axis, but the continuous column gives
the zone no width on the other axis. Each zone would span the whole panel, and
the continuous column would be dropped. gog refuses the sentence, and the
message names three ways to fix it. Cut the number into ranges with
`zone * bin * mean`, as in the
[summary heatmap](#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap). Or [declare
the column's categories](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories) before
plotting. A cell that then holds more than one row needs `zone * mean`. Without
it gog refuses the sentence, because each cell would show only its last row. Or
leave the position out of the zone, so each slot spans the panel, as in the
[column highlight](#one-slot-a-column-highlight):

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone + x(year) + y(continent) + color(life)
```

One column is not a pair. The refusal names the column you gave, because a
missing half is nearly always a typo:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower = lower) +
  line
```

On a categorical axis, a number in a pair is a position among the slots: 0 is
the center of the first category's slot, 1 of the second, and so on. The
[waterfall](#the-waterfall)'s `left` and `right` are numbers of this kind. Write
the waterfall's `base` and `top` in the `start`/`end` pair instead. Most of its
blocks would then be far past the sixth slot, outside the panel, so gog refuses
the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(cash_blocks) + zone * bounds(start = base, end = top) + x(step)
```

The message suggests the other pair, `bounds(base, top)`, which bounds the
measure axis.

A zone needs two answers: where its cells are, and what each cell shows.
`bounds` answers only where. `count` and `proportion` answer only what, inside
the cells your categories already make. `density` answers both. `bin` answers
both, and it can also answer only where, which is how `bin * mean` works. Two
transforms that answer the same question contradict each other, as
`bounds * bin` does below. `bounds * mean` is refused for a different reason.
`bounds` makes one rectangle per row, and `mean` one per cell of the positions,
so they disagree about which rectangles there are:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * mean +
  line
```

To shade a region the data *computed* rather than one you chose, use
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), the mark that fills between two computed values:
`ribbon * range` fills between the minimum and maximum at each x. With `bounds`,
a zone shades where you say. A ribbon shades between values a transform computed
from the rows.

Asking for two measurements is also a contradiction. `count` writes one
measurement and `mean` writes another, but a cell holds a single number. `count`
cuts nothing, so with `mean` measuring the cells there is
nothing left for it to do:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)
```

`bin * mean` in [the summary
heatmap](#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap) has the same shape and
is not a contradiction: `bin` supplies the cells, and `mean`
supplies the measurement inside them.

Say `mean` with no column to reduce and gog asks for one rather than guessing.
A zone measures by `color`, so `color` is the binding the refusal names:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season)
```

Naming the sides and cutting them in one sentence is refused, not settled by
picking one, because the named sides and the cut cells would not agree:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * bin +
  line
```

A `bin` needs *something to cut*, and two categorical axes leave it nothing:
each category is one slot, and a slot cannot be cut smaller. The refusal goes
further: a cell per pair
of *categories* is the tile plot, which does no binning at all, so it names the
transform that tallies into cells you already have:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(six_weeks) + zone * bin + x(weekday) + y(week)
```

With one categorical axis and one continuous axis, the sentence draws. That is [the mixed
mesh](#one-of-each-the-mixed-mesh). `density` differs from `bin` here, and the
reason is the estimate itself. A field is estimated *between* the data points,
so it needs somewhere to spread on both axes. A density per category would be
normalized inside each slot on its own, which makes its cells incomparable
across slots, though one color ramp would make them look comparable. A density
per category is a different plot, so gog asks for two continuous axes and names
what to use instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * density + x(life) + y(continent)
```

A tiling is refused for a reason of its own, and that reason is distance. A
hexagon is regular only when a step up and a step across can be compared, so
`hex` needs a *distance* on both axes. A category's slots have an order but no
distance, so a mixed mesh always has rectangular cells:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(life) + y(continent)
```

`count` over continuous axes is the opposite of `bin` over two categorical
axes, and it is refused by the same rule. A tally needs cells that exist; a
number is a point and owns none, so the refusal names `bin`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * count + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

The six summaries follow the same rule. `mean` reduces a column inside a cell,
and a continuous position gives it no cell. The refusal names both fixes: a
category on each position, or `bin` on the continuous axis first:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(bearing) + y(season) + color(speed)
```

And the cells' measure is already the count. Binning turns each cell's rows
into one count, so no other column is left to color by:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

A tiling gog does not offer is refused with the list of the ones it does,
rather than quietly drawing rectangles instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "octagon") + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

`density`'s `bandwidth` is refused here for a reason of its own. It is a width
in one column's own units, and a field spreads over two columns measuring
different quantities, so one number cannot be a width in both. That is why
`adjust` is the parameter [the density
section](#cells-the-data-estimated-zone-density) uses: a multiplier means the
same thing on either axis.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length)
```

## In short {#in-short}

A zone's sides come from five places: `bounds`, `bin`, `density`, a category's
slot, or a boundary named by `group`. `partition` and `flow` compute whole
rectangles themselves. Where nothing gives sides, the zone
reaches the panel edge, which a `ribbon` cannot do. The pair you name decides
which axis it bounds; the column types decide which one measures.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A zone shows a measure as a color, and you read its value from the legend.
[Surface](surface.qmd) gives that measure a height instead, and the same field
is raised into the cube as a sheet.
